title: Tour de France 2027: What Do Extra TT Kms Mean for Evenepoel’s Prospects?
author: sstokes
text:
Can two time trials in the 2027 Tour de France be the key to victory for Remco Evenepoel? (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images) (Photo: Tim De Waele)

Third in 2024, second this year. Is Remco Evenepoel heading towards victory in the 2027 Tour de France ?

His 6:26 deficit to Tadej Pogačar this time around suggests otherwise, but there are three factors which could narrow the gap considerably.

Firstly, there’s Pogačar’s big crash at the Vuelta a España. He suffered a concussion plus fractures to his neck and shoulder, and was forced to abandon the defense of his world and European championship titles.

While the Tour is still over eight months away, Tour de France race director Christian Prudhomme has suggested that fall might have a long-term effect on the five-time winner.

Correct or not, it’s clear his injuries and his curtailed season were less than ideal.

The second factor is the age gap between the two riders. Pogačar is now 28 and, if he follows the usual pattern seen with many athletes, he could see his performances start to plateau.

Evenepoel is a year and four months younger and, at 26, should continue to improve.

The third consideration is the gift the Tour de France organizers handed Evenepoel this week. Namely, the most time trial kilometers to feature in the race since 2012.

This year’s Tour had just 26.1 individual kilometers against the clock.

Next July will see more than double that, with the two TT’s totaling 71km.

That, plus the fact that there are just three summit finishes, two less than this season, means that Evenepoel will feel good about his chances.

While the Belgian was not at this week’s Tour presentation, his Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team gave a big thumbs up to the route.

Directeur sportif Zak Dempster referenced the two races against the clock and said those will help fight for the maillot jaune.

“The first week promises intense racing, where staying out of trouble will be key,” he said.

“The long ITT (individual time trial) at the end of that first week offers us a great opportunity to make an early statement right away. This could be crucial heading into the Alps in the second week.”

And while Evenepoel will then be up against Pogačar and the other favorites in the high mountains, he has a chance to gain further time in the other ITT.

“The second time trial is another highlight of this route,” Dempster continued.

“We welcome the return of more individual time trial kilometers, as this adds another dimension to the race and makes the battle for yellow even more open and exciting. Overall, it’s a route that plays to our strengths and gives us every reason to aim for yellow.”

As for team CEO Ralph Denk, he too was upbeat.

“Remco is the best time triallist at the moment, world champion, and definitely he would be happy. We have two time trials here, more than 70k in TT,” he told VTM Nieuws .

However Denk played down suggestions that three rather than five mountain-top finishes made it an easier Tour in terms of climbing.

“I see this a bit differently because we have a stage of more than 5000 climbing meters,” he said. “It is a super tough one. And there are other climbs here. Let’s see. Let’s evaluate in detail. I will not confirm this is an easy Tour de France.”

“It is always the goal from our team to battle to the best, and let’s see. But for this answer, we need to have a closer look at the route.”

Evenepoel completed the season with a fine statistic. He rode five individual time trials this season, and he won each of them.

He took the TT at the Tour and also won his fourth world championship title, then defended his European champs crown.

He ended off the year with a resounding victory in the Chrono des Nations TT. Evenepoel finished a staggering 2:11 ahead of Jay Vine (UAE Emirates-XRG) there, and said afterwards that everything came together perfectly.

“The handling, the speed and the feeling of being one with the bike all felt really good. Looking ahead to next year, it was all very promising,” he stated.

That kind of performance is why former professional Jan Bakelandts is predicting huge gains in the Tour.

“Remco is genuinely the best time triallist in the world,” he stated in his HLN.be column . “I wouldn’t rule out him taking two minutes out of Pogačar across those two time trials, provided he can reproduce the level he showed at the world championships.

“That’s crucial: he’ll have to be just as brilliant as he was in Montreal, because Pogačar’s track record in the Tour is also astonishingly strong.”

It’s a valid point. Despite Evenepoel’s far greater pedigree as a TT rider, Pogačar limited his losses to 28 seconds in the Tour’s individual time trial this year.

That was over a distance of 26.1km, meaning he gave up just over one second per kilometer.

If he puts in the same kind of performances across the two TTs next summer he will surrender around one minute 11 seconds.

But others such as five time Tour de France winner Bernard Hinault aren’t so sure.

“This Tour is still too hard for him,” he told Nieuwsblad . “This year he has made a nice progression. He had a lower weight and climbed a lot better. But sharp attacks uphill he does not tolerate. Evenepoel is a steady climber. I think he can win stages next year, especially the two time trials.

“But I don’t believe in the general classification. There’s just one that’s better than the rest. And Pogačar will want revenge for the Vuelta.”

Still, Hinault is aware that nothing is guaranteed in sport. He knows pro cycling very well, but also understands that surprises can happen.

“I could be wrong,” he accepted. “And Evenepoel himself must think that he can make it.”

That possibility will sustain the Belgian over the winter months, giving him focus and additional self-belief as he builds towards 2027 and his best Tour prospects thus far.

title: Why Flying With a Bike is Always a Gamble (And How to Improve Your Odds)
author: Josh Ross
text:

I travel with a bike more than most people, and it terrifies me every single time. After having a Look 795 Blade RS arrive broken in a Scicon AeroComfort case, I went down a deep rabbit hole—talking to the TSA and picking apart the fine print of airline contracts of carriage. Since then, I’ve learned even more by talking to the people who actually design bike luggage. Despite still being absolutely terrified of landing with a broken bike, I’ve learned a lot of info that rarely gets talked about. Here’s what I know about flying with a bike right now.

When you check baggage on a flight, you are agreeing to a contract of carriage. You might occasionally have to explicitly sign a waiver, but typically, you’ll hear nothing about it. You’ve still agreed to it, and if something happens to your bike, you are bound by those terms.

This contract outlines the liability an airline accepts when taking your property. Look carefully, because some airlines exclude bike liability completely, while others cap it at a specific amount that likely won’t cover a replacement frame. That cap drops even lower on international flights. The contract will also dictate what type of case is considered acceptable, and most airlines specify a hard case.

On top of airline rules, the TSA will almost always open your bag because it’s too large to be scanned. When I spoke to Sean Harbaugh, a supervisory TSA officer with 20 years of experience, he told me their biggest request is that cyclists stop packing extra gear and clothing into the case alongside the bike.

Add all of this up, and the reality is far less black and white than the airlines want you to believe—a gray area I’ll explain in a moment. But first, if your bike gets damaged, expect a huge fight to get a payout, and it will likely be less than you need. Regardless of the amount though, if you want any chance of succeeding, you must check your bike at the airport before you leave. You cannot make a claim once you walk out those doors. Open the case, check carefully for damage, and start the claim immediately if you find a problem. During that process, explicitly request that the security video of the TSA checking your bike be preserved. The inspection is always on video, but that footage will be overwritten unless you demand they pull it.

This is pretty obvious, and it’s what everyone thinks is the issue. Baggage handlers generally do not care about your bike. Sometimes they are outright hostile with it, but typically, they just don’t care. The bag will almost always get flipped on its side, and it will sometimes get slammed on the ground, a luggage cart, or a belt. Make sure whatever case you use will protect your bike from this treatment.

If your bars come off and you can fold them down, things are pretty easy. Even a cardboard box will typically work, although my favorite option for this scenario is the Topeak PakGo X. The real challenge comes when you are dealing with a modern bike and can’t take your bars off.

If that’s what you are up against, look for something that keeps your case from being crushed from the sides. The Orucase Sentinel is an incredible option that uses a rather genius internal aluminum roll cage. It protects the controls by running a rigid expansion bar through the drops that secures into place inside the case. I have a friend who actually uses the Scicon that broke my bike, but he uses PVC pipes to create an anti-crush system very similar to what Orucase is doing. Of course, a more traditional hard case will win out if you are only looking at what it takes to protect your bike from the baggage handlers.

After I had my bike broken, I swore I’d never fly with another soft case. Then I started using the Orucase Sentinel and had a conversation with the founder of Orucase, Isaac Howe. I’ve talked to him for years about the theory of bike cases, but recently we talked about what actually constitutes a “hard case.”

In talking to him, I realized I’d made a mistake in blindly believing the airlines. It seems like what the contract of carriage means is that you need a giant plastic or aluminum vault like a Shokbox or a Bike Box Alan. The reality is that no one has ever litigated it. If you have a soft outer material that covers a rigid internal structure, you can argue that it is still a hard case. Should someone go to court with that line of reasoning, they might well win. No one will actually go to court, though, so my advice is to think carefully about what you say if you ever make a claim. Your case could well qualify as a hard case, so don’t make the mistake of calling it a soft case.

The reason all of this matters is that you aren’t just protecting your bike from baggage handlers. If you were, a traditional hard case would be the undisputed answer. Instead, Howe told me that one of the hardest things to design for is the TSA. You meticulously pack your bike, everything is safe inside a hard outer shell, and then a TSA agent opens it and doesn’t bother putting it back together correctly. You might end up with a broken bike even though the case was strong enough to withstand anything a baggage handler could throw at it.

For my most recent trip, I ended up choosing the Post Carry Co. Loomer for this exact reason. It helped that Factor CEO Calvin Chan told me he carries the Factor ONE Bugatti edition bikes all over the world in that case, but it was also just the way it works. It’s essentially a hard case, but its simple closure system and the ease of seeing the bike made me think the TSA might be less apt to mess it up.…
